title: The Desktop Frontier — Ahmad Osman, Osmantic
talk_summary: Ahmad Osman argues that open-weight models are rapidly densifying—capability per parameter is improving so fast that models like Qwen 3.6 27B now beat much larger older models—and predicts frontier-class intelligence on a single RTX 5090 within ~18 months. The talk is mostly a hardware-sovereignty pitch (buy GPUs, self-host) with benchmark anecdotes rather than operational techniques.

takeaways.technique: Re-benchmark cheap models on your own tasks periodically
takeaways.what_they_do: Tracks how newer smaller open models overtake older larger ones on benchmarks, arguing capability density improves ~50% per 3.5 months, so model choice should be revisited often.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It's not that small models are beating big models. It's that newer, more efficient models are beating older, less efficient ones.
takeaways.numbers: Qwen 3.6 27B dense reportedly beats Qwen 3.5 397B MoE; ~50% parameter-efficiency gain every 3.5 months (cited 'densing law')

takeaways.technique: Prefer dense small models for high-volume agent loops
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues dense ~27B models with high activated-parameter ratios deliver near-MoE quality at a fraction of the footprint, making them viable for many parallel agents.
takeaways.evidence_quote: those same eight RTX3090s could run something like 15 parallel agents right now with Quen 3.5 27
takeaways.numbers: 8x RTX3090 running ~15 parallel agents on a 27B model

takeaways.technique: Own/self-host inference hardware for steady load
takeaways.what_they_do: Pitches buying a DGX-station-class box to run open-weight models locally so you control cost and availability instead of paying subsidized cloud tokens that may later rise.
takeaways.evidence_quote: why are you funding other people to build data centers so that you can subscribe to them and pay subsidized tokens
